title: Two cases of steroid dementia showing partial recovery during 2‐year follow‐up
journal: PCN Reports: Psychiatry and Clinical Neurosciences
case_prompt: A 68-year-old woman with Hashimoto’s disease and anti–aminoacyl t-RNA synthetase antibody–positive interstitial lung disease was prescribed prednisolone, 60 mg daily. Forty-five days later, she became confused when performing routine tasks such as bathing and operating the television. Her Hasegawa’s Dementia Scale–Revised score was 24 (dementia cutoff, ≤20). Electroencephalography showed no slow-wave activity, and 3-T magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed no atrophy or abnormal signals. The prednisolone dose was tapered to 30 mg daily, and after discharge she exhibited behavioral disturbances, including wearing excessive clothing and eating all the food in the refrigerator. There were no overt psychiatric symptoms. On readmission, thyroid function tests were normal. Repeated EEG again showed no abnormal waves, and brain MRI remained normal. Her Hasegawa’s Dementia Scale–Revised score had declined to 17. Disorientation, short-term and long-term memory disturbance, and loss of episodic memory were observed, while consciousness remained clear.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Hashimoto’s encephalopathy was considered but excluded — “No slow waves in EEG and no abnormal findings in brain MRI ruled out Hashimoto’s encephalopathy.”  
2. Steroid-induced psychiatric disorder (steroid psychosis) was considered but excluded — “There were no obvious steroid-induced psychiatric symptoms.”  
3. Delirium was considered but excluded — “Consciousness was not altered, and repeated EEG showed no abnormal waves … suggesting no existence of delirium.”  
4. Neurodegenerative dementia (e.g., Alzheimer disease) was considered but deemed unlikely — “No obvious brain atrophy or abnormal signals shown by 3T MRI.”
